title: The Universe · Episode 2
chapters: Ocean moons: hidden seas of the outer solar system
Comets: dirty snowballs from the deep

units.t: The Universe. Episode two.
In this episode: Ocean moons: hidden seas of the outer solar system, Pluto and the dwarf planets, Comets: dirty snowballs from the deep and Shooting stars and meteorites.
Part one. Ocean moons: hidden seas of the outer solar system.
Some of the best places to look for alien life may be dark oceans hidden beneath the ice of moons orbiting Jupiter and Saturn.
Hidden seas, tidal heat.
Out past Mars, sunlight is weak and the surface of Jupiter's and Saturn's moons sits well below minus 100 degrees Celsius.
Yet spacecraft show that several of these moons appear to hide global oceans of liquid water beneath shells of ice.
Europa may hold more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.
How does water stay liquid?
Mainly through tidal heating.
These moons follow slightly oval orbits around giant planets, so the pull of gravity changes and squeezes and stretches them.
Like a paperclip bent back and forth, they warm by friction.
Jupiter's Io is the extreme case, the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
Gentler heating, plus heat from radioactive elements in the rock, appears enough to keep oceans liquid under kilometres of ice.
Europa's hidden ocean.
Europa is slightly smaller than our Moon, but its surface is bright white ice crisscrossed by reddish brown cracks, with very few craters.
That means the surface is young and constantly reshaped.
In the late 1990s NASA's Galileo spacecraft measured how Europa disturbed Jupiter's magnetic field, and the best explanation was a salty, electrically conducting ocean under the ice.
The ice shell is thought to be several to a few dozen kilometres thick, over an ocean perhaps around 100 kilometres deep.
Crucially, that ocean probably sits on a rocky seafloor.
Water and rock could react chemically there, as they do around hydrothermal vents in Earth's deep oceans, where life thrives without sunlight.
Enceladus geysers.
Enceladus is only about 500 kilometres across, small enough to fit within the width of Victoria, so scientists expected little.
Then in 2005 NASA's Cassini spacecraft spotted jets of water vapour and ice grains erupting from long cracks near its south pole, nicknamed tiger stripes.
The plumes feed one of Saturn's rings.
Cassini later flew straight through them, essentially tasting an alien ocean.
It found water, salts, carbon dioxide, ammonia and organic molecules.
Tiny silica grains hinted at hot water reacting with rock on the seafloor, and later analysis found phosphorus, an essential ingredient for life on Earth.
Enceladus appears to tick many boxes for habitability: liquid water, chemical energy and the right raw materials.
Titan and Ganymede.
Saturn's Titan is bigger than Mercury and the only moon with a thick atmosphere, mostly nitrogen.
At around minus 180 degrees Celsius, water is rock-hard, but methane and ethane flow as liquids.
Titan has clouds, rain, rivers and seas of liquid hydrocarbons.
In 2005 Europe's Huygens probe parachuted through the orange haze and landed on a damp plain strewn with rounded ice pebbles.
Measurements suggest a water ocean lies deep below.
Jupiter's Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system and the only one known to generate its own magnetic field.
Hubble observations of its shifting auroras suggest a salty ocean beneath the surface.
Callisto may have one too, and oceans are suspected further out, including Triton and Pluto.
Missions and caution.
If buried oceans are common, liquid water may be far more widespread in the universe than on sunlit rocky planets like Earth, greatly increasing the number of places life could arise.
Several spacecraft are on their way.
ESA's JUICE, launched in 2023, will study Jupiter's icy moons and eventually orbit Ganymede.
NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will make dozens of close flybys of Europa.
NASA's Dragonfly, a nuclear-powered rotorcraft, is planned to fly between sites on Titan in the 2030s.
Scientists take great care not to contaminate these worlds with Earth microbes, a principle called planetary protection.
That is why Galileo was deliberately plunged into Jupiter in 2003, and Cassini into Saturn in 2017, as their fuel ran low.
The key idea: Several icy moons hide liquid oceans, kept from freezing by tidal heating as their planet's gravity flexes them.
Part two. Pluto and the dwarf planets.
In 2006 Pluto was voted out of the planet club.
The real story is less about Pluto being demoted and more about discovering it had a lot of company.
Found by patience.
In the early 1900s, astronomer Percival Lowell was convinced an unknown 'Planet X' lay beyond Neptune, and his observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, kept searching after his death.
In 1929 it hired Clyde Tombaugh, a 22-year-old Kansas farm boy with no university degree, who had impressed staff with drawings from his homemade telescope.
Tombaugh photographed the same patches of sky several nights apart and flicked between the plates with a blink comparator, looking for a dot that moved against the background stars.
On 18 February 1930 he found one.
The calculations that inspired the hunt later proved wrong, so finding Pluto was partly luck, combined with enormous patience.
Named by a schoolgirl.
News of the new planet spread worldwide, and name suggestions poured in.
In Oxford, England, 11-year-old Venetia Burney heard about it over breakfast and suggested Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld, fitting for a cold, dark world at the edge of the solar system.
Her grandfather passed the idea to an astronomer friend, who sent it to the Lowell Observatory.
Staff there voted unanimously in favour, partly because the first two letters, P and L, honoured Percival Lowell.
Venetia reportedly received a five-pound note as a reward.
Soon after, Walt Disney introduced a cartoon dog named Pluto.
Decades later, an instrument on the New Horizons spacecraft was named in her honour.
Smaller and smaller.
At discovery, Pluto was assumed to be roughly Earth-sized, because it was thought to be disturbing Neptune's orbit.
Each new measurement shrank it.
In 1978 astronomers discovered its largest moon, Charon, which allowed Pluto's mass to be calculated precisely.
It was tiny: only about a fifth of our Moon's mass.
Pluto is about 2,380 kilometres across, narrower than Australia is wide.
Charon is about half Pluto's diameter, so large that the two swing around a shared point in the space between them.
Pluto's orbit is also odd: stretched and tilted, and between 1979 and 1999 it came closer to the Sun than Neptune did.
A crowded neighbourhood.
In 1992 astronomers found another small icy body beyond Neptune, the first known member of what is now called the Kuiper Belt.
Hundreds, then thousands more followed.
Pluto was not a lonely ninth planet but one of the largest of a vast belt of frozen leftovers.
The crisis came in 2005, when a team led by Mike Brown announced Eris, first thought larger than Pluto.
Later measurements showed it is very slightly smaller in diameter but about a quarter more massive.
If Pluto was a planet, Eris had to be one too, and possibly dozens more.
In August 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet in Prague: it orbits the Sun, is massive enough to be round, and has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.
Pluto has a heart.
Pluto passes the first two tests but fails the third, because it shares its region with countless Kuiper Belt objects.
It became a dwarf planet, alongside Eris and the asteroid Ceres, with Haumea and Makemake added later.
Some planetary scientists still argue for a definition based on a body's own properties, not its surroundings.
NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015, nine and a half years after launch.
Expectations were modest: an old, cratered ball of ice.
Instead it found a pale heart-shaped region, Tombaugh Regio, holding Sputnik Planitia, a young plain of nitrogen ice that flows like glaciers and has almost no craters.
There were also water-ice mountains kilometres high and a blue haze.
Some of Tombaugh's ashes were aboard.
The key idea: Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930 by comparing photographs of the sky, partly through luck and mostly through patience.
Part three. Comets: dirty snowballs from the deep.
For thousands of years comets were seen as omens of doom.
Then one astronomer predicted a comet's return, died before he could see it, and was proved right.
Omens in the sky.
A comet appears suddenly, hangs in the sky for weeks with a ghostly tail, then fades.
To many ancient cultures that unpredictability was frightening.
Chinese astronomers kept careful comet records for more than two thousand years, often linking them to political upheaval.
In 1066 a bright comet appeared over Europe shortly before the Norman conquest of England, and the Bayeux Tapestry shows people pointing at it in alarm.
The word comet comes from the Greek for 'long-haired', describing the streaming tail.
Aristotle believed comets were something happening in Earth's upper atmosphere, not objects travelling through space.
It took many centuries, and better telescopes, to prove him wrong.
Halley's bold prediction.
In the early 1700s, the English astronomer Edmond Halley studied records of bright comets and noticed that those seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 had remarkably similar paths.
Using his friend Isaac Newton's new laws of gravity, he argued they were a single comet on a long oval orbit, returning roughly every 75 to 76 years.
He predicted it would reappear around 1758.
Halley died in 1742 and never saw the result.
On Christmas night 1758, a German farmer and amateur astronomer, Johann Palitzsch, spotted the comet right on cue.
It was a triumph for Newton's physics, and the comet has carried Halley's name ever since.
It last passed in 1986 and is due back in 2061.
A dirty snowball.
In 1950 the American astronomer Fred Whipple proposed that a comet's heart, its nucleus, is a 'dirty snowball' of frozen water, carbon dioxide, ammonia and other ices mixed with dust and rock.
Space missions have since confirmed the basic idea, though many comets turned out to be more dust than ice.
A typical nucleus is only a few kilometres wide and surprisingly dark, reflecting about as much light as charcoal.
When the European probe Giotto flew past Halley's Comet in 1986, it photographed a lumpy, peanut-shaped nucleus roughly 15 kilometres long, jetting gas from its sunlit side.
The display we see from Earth comes not from this tiny core but from the vast cloud it releases when warmed.
Two tails, not one.
Far from the Sun a comet is frozen and inactive.
As it swings closer, sunlight warms the surface and the ices turn straight into gas, dragging dust out with them.
This builds a fuzzy atmosphere called the coma, which can be larger than Jupiter.
Then the tails form.
The dust tail is pushed gently by sunlight, curves along the comet's path and shines yellowish white.
The ion tail is made of electrically charged gas swept away by the solar wind, so it runs straight and often glows blue.
Here is the surprise: both tails point away from the Sun, not behind the comet.
When a comet heads back out into the solar system, it travels tail first.
Origins and Rosetta.
Comets are leftovers from the formation of the solar system about 4.
6 billion years ago.
Those returning in under 200 years mostly come from the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune.
Comets with orbits of thousands or millions of years are thought to come from the Oort Cloud, a vast shell of icy objects.
No one has directly seen it; it is inferred from the orbits of comets.
The European Space Agency's Rosetta reached comet 67P, a rubber-duck-shaped body about four kilometres long, after a ten-year chase.
In November 2014 it released the Philae lander.
Its harpoons failed to fire, and it bounced twice into a cliff's shadow, yet sent data for about 60 hours.
Rosetta found 67P's water differs chemically from Earth's oceans.
The key idea: Before science explained them, comets were widely feared as signs of disaster, and even Aristotle misjudged what they were.
Part four. Shooting stars and meteorites.
Most shooting stars are specks of dust smaller than a grain of rice, yet a few space rocks survive the fall and carry chemistry older than the Sun.
Not really a star.
Lie on your back somewhere dark for half an hour and you will probably see a few shooting stars.
Despite the name, they have nothing to do with stars.
Each one is a piece of rock or dust, often no bigger than a grain of sand, hitting the atmosphere at roughly 11 to 72 kilometres per second.
It heats the air so violently that it vaporises and makes the air glow, usually 70 to 100 kilometres up.
Astronomers use three words.
A meteoroid drifts in space.
A meteor is the glowing streak.
A meteorite is any piece that survives and lands on the ground.
Why showers return.
On most nights you might see a handful of random meteors an hour.
On certain dates each year the count jumps, sometimes to dozens an hour.
These are meteor showers, and they arrive like clockwork because Earth crosses the same streams of debris at the same point in its orbit.
Most streams were shed by comets as they swung past the Sun.
Halley's Comet, for example, feeds two showers: the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October.
The meteors seem to fly out from one point, the radiant, and the shower is named after the constellation it sits in.
It is a perspective effect, like parallel railway lines appearing to meet in the distance.
Showers for Australians.
Some famous showers favour the north.
The Perseids in August are low or invisible from much of Australia.
Southern observers do better with the Eta Aquariids, peaking in early May, whose radiant rises higher in our pre-dawn sky.
The Geminids, peaking around the middle of December, are among the richest showers of the year.
Unusually, they come from an asteroid called Phaethon rather than a comet.
For any shower, get away from city lights, let your eyes adjust for at least 20 minutes and lie back to take in as much sky as possible.
Counts are usually best after midnight, when your side of Earth faces forward into the debris stream.
Rocks from the sky.
Meteorites come in three families.
Stony ones are the most common, and many are chondrites containing round grains formed in the dust cloud that built the planets about 4.
6 billion years ago.
Iron meteorites are metal chunks, thought to come from the cores of shattered asteroids.
Stony-iron ones mix both.
On 28 September 1969 a meteorite broke up over Murchison in Victoria.
It contains amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and grains older than the Sun itself.
Very large rocks barely notice the air and blast out craters, like the 880-metre Wolfe Creek Crater in Western Australia.
In 2013 a roughly 20-metre object exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, and flying glass injured around 1,500 people.
Found a space rock.
Australia's deserts are excellent meteorite hunting grounds.
Dark rocks stand out on pale ground, and the dry climate slows weathering.
Curtin University's Desert Fireball Network uses cameras to photograph bright fireballs so their landing spots can be calculated and fragments recovered.
If you think you have found one, look for a rock that feels unusually heavy for its size, often attracts a magnet and has a thin, dark, glassy crust from melting during its fall.
Real meteorites rarely have bubbly holes.
Most candidates turn out to be iron-rich Earth rocks or industrial slag, nicknamed meteorwrongs.
State museums can often identify specimens, and in some states meteorites legally belong to the state, so check the rules before selling one.
The key idea: A shooting star is a speck of space rock or dust burning up in the atmosphere, and it lands as a meteorite only if part survives.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What mainly keeps these moons' oceans from freezing?
Answer. Heat from tidal flexing by their planet's gravity.
Question two. How did Clyde Tombaugh find Pluto?
Answer. By comparing photographs for a dot that moved.
Question three. How did many ancient cultures see comets?
Answer. As frightening signs of disaster.
Question four. Which description fits a meteorite?
Answer. A space rock that survives and lands on Earth.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
